request.system:
You are the extractor in Ledger, a system that documents legacy COBOL business rules so that a modern port can be written from the rules alone and checked against the running original.

Write business rules as Given/When/Then scenarios in plain English that a policy owner can read and approve. Hard requirements:

- Every clause cites the exact source lines it comes from (file plus [first, last] line numbers from the numbered listing; keep spans tight, normally 1-12 lines). If a statement cannot be sourced to specific lines, leave it out.
- When a fact needs a second place, add it under "also" (at most 2 extra spans, each with its own file and [first, last]). Typical case: the statement in the program that does something (a COMPUTE, a reference modification like (1:10), a MOVE) plus the field's PIC declaration in a copybook that fixes its size or precision. A clause is judged only on the lines it cites, so cite every line its claim depends on.
- Every clause lists the COBOL data names ("fields") and literal values ("literals": codes, messages, constants, without quotes) it relies on. Each listed field and literal must literally appear in one of the cited spans; a checker will reject the clause otherwise. Cite a declaration line (for example a PIC clause in WORKING-STORAGE) when the clause depends on a field's size or precision.
- Describe what the code actually does, not what it was probably meant to do. If the code has surprising behaviour (a later check overwriting an earlier result, a branch that can never run, arithmetic that truncates, a check that ignores something), state that behaviour precisely in the rule.
- Separate business logic from file plumbing. Opening/closing files, file-status checks, and abend handling are plumbing; leave them out unless they change a business outcome. Balance and record updates (for example 2700-*, 2800-*, 1050-* paragraphs) are business logic: a port that skips them would produce different output files.
- Be precise enough that a developer who never sees the COBOL could reproduce the outputs exactly: name the output fields set, the exact codes and message texts, the order of checks, signs and arithmetic (COBOL truncates toward zero unless ROUNDED is written), and which records are created versus updated.
- Keep each clause to one checkable fact. When a fact depends on a record layout, field size or precision, put it in its own clause that cites the declaration. Do not restate in one clause what another clause (or another part of the program) establishes.
- Keep rules small: at most 8 clauses per rule. If a behaviour needs more, keep only the clauses that change the program's outputs.
- Do not write clauses that claim something is absent or never happens ("never checks the active status", "the counter is never reset", "no other code reads it"). Cited lines cannot prove an absence. Put such observations in "notes" instead; notes are shown to the reviewer as unverified and are not given to the port.
- Use the field names exactly as declared. Use the tools to read any other paragraph or field layout you need; do not guess line numbers.

Return only rules for the unit you are given, at most the number requested, each one a distinct behaviour with an observable effect on the program's outputs.

When the account ID changes, the account loaded before is written back with its interest (except on the very first record), the interest total is reset to zero, and the new account and its card cross-reference are read. Every record, including the first of a group, then goes on to rate lookup, and interest is only calculated when the rate is not zero.","given":[{"text":"Category balance records are read one at a time from the indexed category balance file, in key order. On the first group the first-time flag is just set to 'N'.","file":"CBACT04C.cbl","lines":[195,199],"also":[],"fields":["WS-FIRST-TIME"],"literals":["Y","N"]},{"text":"The interest total is reset to 0 and the last-seen account number is set to the new account ID.","file":"CBACT04C.cbl","lines":[200,201],"also":[],"fields":["WS-TOTAL-INT","WS-LAST-ACCT-NUM","TRANCAT-ACCT-ID"],"literals":["0"]},{"text":"The account record for the new account ID is read by key from the account file into ACCOUNT-RECORD.","file":"CBACT04C.cbl","lines":[202,203],"also":[{"file":"CBACT04C.cbl","lines":[372,376]}],"fields":["TRANCAT-ACCT-ID","FD-ACCT-ID","ACCOUNT-RECORD"],"literals":[]},{"text":"The card cross-reference for the account is read through the account-ID alternate key. This supplies the card number that later goes on the interest transactions.","file":"CBACT04C.cbl","lines":[204,205],"also":[{"file":"CBACT04C.cbl","lines":[393,398]}],"fields":["TRANCAT-ACCT-ID","FD-XREF-ACCT-ID","CARD-XREF-RECORD"],"literals":[]},{"text":"For every category balance record, whether or not the account changed, the rate lookup key is built from the account's group ID and the record's category code and type code, and the interest rate is looked up.","file":"CBACT04C.cbl","lines":[210,213],"also":[],"fields":["ACCT-GROUP-ID","FD-DIS-ACCT-GROUP-ID","TRANCAT-CD","FD-DIS-TRAN-CAT-CD","TRANCAT-TYPE-CD","FD-DIS-TRAN-TYPE-CD"],"literals":[]},{"text":"Interest is calculated (and the fee step run) only when the interest rate found is not zero.
